newsitem.title: GREECE: Candidates to clash in Greece's first TV debate.
newsitem.headline: Candidates to clash in Greece's first TV debate.

text.p: For the first time in Greece, the two lead candidates for prime minister will face off in a U.S.- style television debate on Friday, hoping to lure undecided voters in what the press has dubbed the "couch elections".

Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis and conservative opposition leader Miltiadis Evert agreed to the prime-time TV duel as opinion polls show them running neck-and-neck 10 days before the September 22 vote.

About 20 percent of those asked nationwide in most polls said they were still unsure of how they would cast their ballot, showing that many Greek voters are unusually apathetic, uninspired by the issues and personalities in the race.
Officials at Simitis' PASOK party said the pro-European technocrat will try to focus his presentation on Greece's future and prospects in the European Union.
"He will emphasize the fact he is a responsible politician with clear positions and views," a PASOK official said. "He will avoid impressive gestures and direct arguments with Evert."

The conservative New Democracy (ND) camp, which is carefully coaching its leader ahead of the debate, said Evert would have preferred a more direct dialogue on TV rather than the U.S.-style question and answer debate.
"But it takes two to tango and Simitis was afraid all his arguments would be shot down by Evert," said George Levidis, ND's foreign press spokesman.
Evert, a stocky 57-year-old who delights in being described as "the bulldozer", is the complete visual opposite of Simitis, 60, who is slightly built and softly-spoken.
Both had opted for a modern, media-oriented campaign, defying the styles of their predecessors who enjoyed rousing huge crowds in public squares across Greece.

But analysts said the new campaign style may be less effective than Greece's new generation of politicians had hoped for and that Greeks may still want to shake hands with the person they will vote for.

Both contenders still do some local campaigning but it is a far cry from the traditional fiery balcony speeches to hundreds of thousands of eager supporters screaming prepared slogans and waving plastic party flags.
"The Socialists are realising that people need to touch their candidates and have modified their tactics, multiplying their tours of the countryside," one pollster said.
Simitis, who called the snap election confident he was leading the polls, had an early advantage but the conservatives have been coming on strong.
His camp hopes the TV debate will help his standing but does not feel it will be a critical factor in the race.
"Any good presentation helps but voters will judge by the overall picture," one of his advisors said.
The debate will start at 1800 GMT on Friday and last for more than an hour. It will be televised live by all channels.
A coordinator will direct questions by three journalists to the two candidates, who will each have two minutes to answer the same question.
